explanations.explanation: That's the one, friend. Paul opens with "To Timothy, my beloved child…" (2 Timothy 1:2). Before he asks for anything or teaches anything, he says how much Timothy means to him. A letter that starts with love gets read twice.

Close, because Paul does call Timothy a fellow worker elsewhere (Romans 16:21). But in this verse he writes "To Timothy, my beloved child…" (2 Timothy 1:2). It's warmer than brother. I think that tells you how close the two of them were.

I get why you'd pick it, since Paul trusts Timothy with a lot in this letter. But the verse says "To Timothy, my beloved child…" (2 Timothy 1:2). Paul doesn't open with a job title. He opens with love, and that's a better way to start any letter.
Yep. Paul says, "…as I constantly remember you night and day in my prayers." (2 Timothy 1:3). Night AND day, friend. I think that's what being loved looks like.

This one is true, friend. Paul writes, "…as I constantly remember you night and day in my prayers." (2 Timothy 1:3). He doesn't just think of Timothy now and then. Night and day, he's praying for him.

That's right. Paul writes, "Recalling your tears, I long to see you so that I may be filled with joy." (2 Timothy 1:4). He remembers Timothy's tears and he misses him. Seeing Timothy is what he says would fill him with joy.

It's actually true, friend. Paul says, "Recalling your tears, I long to see you so that I may be filled with joy." (2 Timothy 1:4). Seeing Timothy would fill Paul with joy. He's not just writing a polite letter here, he's missing his friend.

You got it, baker. Paul says the faith "…first dwelt in your grandmother Lois and your mother Eunice…" (2 Timothy 1:5). Lois is the grandmother and Eunice is the mother. It lived in them first, and Paul is convinced it's in Timothy as well.

Priscilla and Aquila were a married couple who worked with Paul (Acts 18:2-3), so good guess. But in this verse, Paul names "…your grandmother Lois and your mother Eunice…" (2 Timothy 1:5). Those are the two whose faith came first. Next time, look for the family members.

Martha welcomed Jesus into her home, and she had a sister named Mary (Luke 10:38-39). They're wonderful, but they aren't in this letter. Paul says the faith first lived in "…your grandmother Lois and your mother Eunice…" (2 Timothy 1:5). Those two women were Timothy's own family.
That's it, friend. Paul says, "…fan into flame the gift of God, which is in you…" (2 Timothy 1:6). You fan a fire to make it burn bright. Don't let it sit there and sulk.
Nope, Paul says the opposite. He tells Timothy to "…fan into flame the gift of God…" (2 Timothy 1:6). Resting and cooling is how a fire turns into a sad pile of ash. Paul wants this one burning.

I see the thinking, since Paul does talk about guarding something later (2 Timothy 1:14). But here he says to "…fan into flame the gift of God…" (2 Timothy 1:6). A flame needs air, and you can't fan something that's shut in a jar. Fanning it into flame is the instruction Paul gives.

That's the word, friend. "For God has not given us a spirit of fear, but of power, love, and self-control." (2 Timothy 1:7). A spirit of fear isn't what God has given us. Power, love and self-control are, and that's a much better bag of gifts.

Joy is a good word, and Paul does talk about being filled with joy in verse 4. But verse 7 says, "For God has not given us a spirit of fear, but of power, love, and self-control." (2 Timothy 1:7). The blank is the thing God did NOT give us. That one is fear.

Truth is a fine word, but it's not the one Paul wrote here. The verse says, "For God has not given us a spirit of fear, but of power, love, and self-control." (2 Timothy 1:7). The blank is the thing God has not given. That's fear.
Right on, baker. Paul says, "So do not be ashamed of the testimony of our Lord…" (2 Timothy 1:8). That's the first thing he names. Then he adds a second thing, so keep reading.

Not this time. Paul says, "So do not be ashamed of the testimony of our Lord, or of me, His prisoner." (2 Timothy 1:8). Traditions of fathers never show up in that line. The first thing he names is the testimony of our Lord.

That sounds like it could be in there, but it isn't. The verse says, "So do not be ashamed of the testimony of our Lord, or of me, His prisoner." (2 Timothy 1:8). The first thing he names is the testimony of our Lord. The covenant isn't mentioned in that line.
Yep. Paul writes, "…or of me, His prisoner." (2 Timothy 1:8). He's in chains, and he calls himself the Lord's prisoner. I think that tells you whose prisoner he feels he really is.

It's true, friend. Paul says, "So do not be ashamed of the testimony of our Lord, or of me, His prisoner." (2 Timothy 1:8). He calls himself the Lord's prisoner. He doesn't hide the chains, he just says it.
Look again, friend. Paul says to join him in suffering "…by the power of God." (2 Timothy 1:8). It's not by Timothy's own strength. And that matches verse 7, which says God gave us a spirit of power.

Right, it's false. Paul says, "…join me in suffering for the gospel by the power of God." (2 Timothy 1:8). The strength comes from God, not from Timothy's own muscles. That's good news, because my own muscles are just a mustache.

That's the one, friend. Paul says God saved us and called us "…not because of our works, but by His own purpose and by the grace He granted us in Christ Jesus…" (2 Timothy 1:9). It's all on God's side. His purpose and His grace are what's behind it.

explanations.answer: The good works we have done
explanations.explanation: I see why you'd pick it, but Paul says it's the opposite. God saved us "…not because of our works, but by His own purpose and by the grace He granted us in Christ Jesus…" (2 Timothy 1:9). Our works aren't what's behind it. His purpose and His grace are.

Prayer matters, and Paul prays a lot in this letter. But in this verse, God saved us "…not because of our works, but by His own purpose and by the grace He granted us in Christ Jesus…" (2 Timothy 1:9). The reason Paul gives is God's own purpose and grace.

Yep, that's what the verse says. God's grace was granted to us "…in Christ Jesus before time began." (2 Timothy 1:9). Before time began, friend. That grace was there before the first clock ever ticked.
It's true. Paul writes of "…the grace He granted us in Christ Jesus before time began." (2 Timothy 1:9). Before time began! God's plan wasn't a last-minute thing.
That's the word. Christ Jesus "…has abolished death and illuminated the way to life and immortality through the gospel…" (2 Timothy 1:10). Abolished. That's not a small word. I'd put it on a banner.

War is a heavy word, but it's not the one here. The verse says Christ Jesus "…has abolished death and illuminated the way to life and immortality through the gospel…" (2 Timothy 1:10). What He abolished is death.

Sickness is a real struggle, and I can see why it came to mind. But Paul wrote that Christ Jesus "…has abolished death and illuminated the way to life and immortality through the gospel…" (2 Timothy 1:10). The word is death. And notice how it connects to life and immortality right after.
Not quite, friend. Paul says, "…even though I suffer as I do, I am not ashamed…" (2 Timothy 1:12). He does suffer, and he says so plainly. But the suffering hasn't made him ashamed.
That's right. Paul writes, "…even though I suffer as I do, I am not ashamed…" (2 Timothy 1:12). He's honest about the suffering, and he's just as honest that he isn't ashamed. Both are true at once.

explanations.answer: He knows whom he has believed
explanations.explanation: You got it, baker. Paul says, "for I know whom I have believed, and I am convinced that He is able to guard what I have entrusted to Him for that day." (2 Timothy 1:12). His reason isn't a circumstance. It's a Person he knows.

explanations.answer: He knows his suffering will end soon
explanations.explanation: I see why you'd go there, but Paul never says that. He writes, "for I know whom I have believed, and I am convinced that He is able to guard what I have entrusted to Him for that day." (2 Timothy 1:12). His reason is Who he trusts, not when the hard part ends.

explanations.answer: He knows the church stands with him
explanations.explanation: That would be nice, but it's not his reason. Just a few verses later he says everyone in Asia has deserted him (2 Timothy 1:15). What he says here is, "for I know whom I have believed…" (2 Timothy 1:12). His confidence rests on the Lord, not on a crowd.

explanations.answer: The Holy Spirit who dwells in us
explanations.explanation: That's right, friend. Paul says, "Guard the treasure entrusted to you, with the help of the Holy Spirit who dwells in us." (2 Timothy 1:14). Timothy isn't guarding it alone. The Spirit is helping him.

explanations.answer: The elders who prayed over him
explanations.explanation: Good thought, friend. But for guarding the treasure, Paul says, "…with the help of the Holy Spirit who dwells in us." (2 Timothy 1:14). The help named here is the Holy Spirit.

explanations.answer: The believers who serve beside him
explanations.explanation: Fellow believers are a blessing, no doubt. But Paul's answer in this verse is, "…with the help of the Holy Spirit who dwells in us." (2 Timothy 1:14). The Holy Spirit is the helper he names here.

explanations.answer: He often refreshed Paul and wasn't ashamed of Paul's chains
explanations.explanation: Yep, that's the reason. Paul writes, "…because he has often refreshed me and was unashamed of my chains." (2 Timothy 1:16). Remember Paul told Timothy not to be ashamed of him? Onesiphorus is the one who wasn't.

explanations.answer: He paid a large sum to get Paul released from prison
explanations.explanation: That would make a dramatic story, but the text doesn't say it. Paul gives this reason: "…because he has often refreshed me and was unashamed of my chains." (2 Timothy 1:16). No money is mentioned. Showing up and not being ashamed was the gift.

explanations.answer: He took over teaching the churches Paul had started
explanations.explanation: Not in this letter, friend. Paul's reason is, "…because he has often refreshed me and was unashamed of my chains." (2 Timothy 1:16). Nothing here says he took over any teaching. He refreshed Paul and stood by him.
That's the word. "…when he arrived in Rome, he searched diligently until he found me." (2 Timothy 1:17). Diligently means he kept at it. He didn't stop until he found Paul.

Waiting is a fine thing, but it isn't what Onesiphorus did. The verse says, "…when he arrived in Rome, he searched diligently until he found me." (2 Timothy 1:17). He went looking and he kept looking.
Prayer matters, but that's not the word here. Paul writes, "…when he arrived in Rome, he searched diligently until he found me." (2 Timothy 1:17). Onesiphorus went looking until he found Paul.
Yep. Paul says, "You know very well how much he ministered to me in Ephesus." (2 Timothy 1:18). He's speaking to Timothy there. Paul is reminding him of something Timothy knows very well.
It's true, friend. Paul writes, "You know very well how much he ministered to me in Ephesus." (2 Timothy 1:18). Timothy knows very well. Paul is reminding him of something he already knows.
